Network metrics summarise the structure of a network, either for each individual (node metrics) or for the whole network (global metrics). In bisonR, metrics are calculated for networks drawn from the posterior of the edge model, giving a posterior distribution for each metric.

```{r setup}
library(bisonR)

sim_data <- simulate_bison_model("binary", aggregated = TRUE)
fit_edge <- bison_model(
  (event | duration) ~ dyad(node_1_id, node_2_id),
  data = sim_data$df_sim,
  model_type = "binary_conjugate",
  priors = get_default_priors("binary_conjugate")
)
```

## Extracting metrics

Metrics are calculated with `extract_metric(fit, metric_name)`. The name has two parts: the *target* (`edge`, `node` or `global`) and the *metric*, joined by an underscore, such as `node_strength` or `global_cv`.

```{r}
strength <- extract_metric(fit_edge, "node_strength", num_draws = 1000)
dim(strength)
```

The result has one row per posterior draw and one column per target: one column per node for node metrics (named after the nodes, in the order of the node levels), one per dyad for edge metrics, and a single column for global metrics. These can be summarised in the same way as other posterior samples:

```{r}
t(apply(strength, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)))
```

`plot_metric()` plots the posterior distribution of a metric. Discrete metrics, such as degree, are shown as bar charts:

```{r}
plot_metric(strength[, 1:2], "Strength of node")
```

To use metrics in regression models, use `bison_brm()` (see `vignette("bison_brms")`) rather than summarising them first.

## Weighted and thresholded metrics

Unless stated otherwise, all metrics are calculated on the **weighted** network, using edge weights on the natural scale (probabilities for binary models, rates for count models). For example, `node_strength` is the weighted version of degree.

Some metrics are only defined for networks where edges are either present or absent. These take a **threshold** in square brackets, such as `node_degree[0.2]`: in each posterior draw, edges with a weight at or above the threshold count as present and the rest as absent. For an unweighted version of a weighted metric (such as unweighted density), threshold the network in the same way. Results can be sensitive to the choice of threshold, so it is worth checking whether conclusions change with different values.

## Available metrics

### Edge metrics

| Name | Definition |
|---|---|
| `edge_weight` | The edge weight of each dyad. Natural scale by default; use `transform = FALSE` for the logit (binary) or log (count) scale. |

### Node metrics

| Name | Definition |
|---|---|
| `node_strength` | Sum of the weights of the node's edges. How much a node associates in total. |
| `node_degree[t]` | Number of edges with weight at or above `t`. |
| `node_eigen` | Eigenvector centrality: high when a node has strong edges to nodes that are themselves central. Scaled so the most central node has a value of 1. |
| `node_betweenness` | Betweenness: the number of shortest paths between other pairs of nodes that pass through the node, using 1/weight as the length of each edge (so strong edges are short). |
| `node_closeness` | Closeness: the inverse of the average shortest-path distance from the node to all others, using 1/weight as edge lengths. |
| `node_clustering[t]` | Local clustering coefficient of the network thresholded at `t`: the proportion of pairs of the node's associates that are also associates of each other. Nodes with fewer than two associates get 0. |

### Global metrics

| Name | Definition |
|---|---|
| `global_density` | Mean edge weight across all dyads in the model (weighted density). |
| `global_cv` | Coefficient of variation (SD / mean) of edge weights, also called social differentiation. High values mean relationships vary a lot in strength. |
| `global_std` | Standard deviation of edge weights. |
| `global_diameter` | Length of the longest shortest path between any two nodes, using 1/weight as edge lengths. |
| `global_clustering[t]` | Global clustering coefficient (transitivity) of the network thresholded at `t`: the proportion of connected triples that are closed triangles. |

Global metrics are calculated from the dyads in the model, so dyads that are not in the data are not included.

## Examples

```{r}
degree <- extract_metric(fit_edge, "node_degree[0.5]", num_draws = 500)
plot_metric(degree[, 1], "Degree (threshold 0.5) of node 1")

eigen <- extract_metric(fit_edge, "node_eigen", num_draws = 500)
round(apply(eigen, 2, median), 2)

cv <- extract_metric(fit_edge, "global_cv", num_draws = 1000)
plot_metric(cv, "Social differentiation (CV)")

clustering <- extract_metric(fit_edge, "global_clustering[0.3]", num_draws = 500)
quantile(clustering, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```

## Using other network tools

Other metrics can be calculated with `bison_to_igraph()`, which returns a list of `igraph` networks drawn from the posterior, with edge weights on the natural scale. Calculating a metric for each network gives its posterior distribution:

```{r}
nets <- bison_to_igraph(fit_edge, num_draws = 200)
weighted_clustering <- sapply(nets, function(net) {
  mean(igraph::transitivity(net, type = "barrat"), na.rm = TRUE)
})
quantile(weighted_clustering, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```

Note that some igraph functions ignore edge weights (for example `igraph::assortativity()`). Because every dyad in the model is an edge in every posterior network, these functions give the same value for every draw, so check that a function uses the `weight` edge attribute before applying it to posterior networks.
